Calculate sample size to detect a difference in prevalence between two groups

Source: R/design_difference.R
design_difference.Rd

Design function: given the expected true prevalence in two groups, returns the sample size needed in each group for test_difference() (with its default score test) to detect that difference with the target power; or, given a full design for both groups, returns the power it gives.

Each group has its own arguments, n1, n_sites1, n_per_site1 for group 1 and n2, n_sites2, n_per_site2 for group 2, as in test_difference(). Each group-2 argument defaults to its group-1 value, so for two groups with the same design only the group-1 arguments are needed.

What is solved for – leave out the one quantity you want, the same in both groups:

No sites

Returns the number of people per group.

n_per_site1 (and n_per_site2)

Returns the number of sites per group, the same in both.

n_sites1 (and n_sites2)

Returns the number of people per site, the same in both.

A full design for both groups

Returns the power. For each group give n (no sites), n_sites and n_per_site, or a vector n_per_site with one size per site (for sites of different sizes). Leave power at its default.

When solving, the groups' sizes follow their fixed values: for example, n_sites1 = 10, n_sites2 = 20 gives group 2 twice as many people as group 1.

Usage

design_difference(
  prevalence1,
  prevalence2,
  power = 0.8,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  sensitivity = 1,
  specificity = 1,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  n1 = NULL,
  n2 = n1,
  n_sites1 = NULL,
  n_sites2 = n_sites1,
  n_per_site1 = NULL,
  n_per_site2 = n_per_site1,
  icc = 0
)

Arguments

prevalence1

Expected true prevalence in group 1, in [0, 1].

prevalence2

Expected true prevalence in group 2, in [0, 1]. The two prevalences must differ.

power

Target power, in [0.5, 1); default 0.80. Not used, and not to be given, with a full design.

alternative

Which kind of difference to look for. "two.sided" (default) looks for any difference; "greater" looks for group 1 being higher (requires prevalence1 > prevalence2); "less" looks for group 1 being lower (requires prevalence1 < prevalence2).

sensitivity

Diagnostic sensitivity in (0, 1]; default 1. Assumed the same in both groups.

specificity

Diagnostic specificity in (0, 1]; default 1. Assumed the same in both groups. sensitivity + specificity must exceed 1.

conf_level

Confidence level, in [0.5, 1); default 0.95. The significance level of the test is 1 - conf_level. Below 0.5 the one-sided z value turns negative and the sample size shrinks towards nonsense, so it is not allowed.

n1, n2

Optional whole numbers: the number of people in each group, for a full design with no sites. n2 defaults to n1.

n_sites1, n_sites2

Optional whole numbers: the number of sites in each group. Alone, the function solves for the number of people per site. n_sites2 defaults to n_sites1.

n_per_site1, n_per_site2

Optional: people per site in each group. One whole number (alone, the function solves for the number of sites), or a vector with one size per site, a full design with sites of different sizes (then leave out that group's n_sites). n_per_site2 defaults to n_per_site1.

icc

Intra-cluster correlation, in [0, 1]: one number for both groups, or two, c(group 1, group 2). Default 0 (no clustering). An icc above 0 needs sites in that group.

Value

A list with:

n_per_group

People in each group, c(group 1, group 2). With sites, n_sites * n_per_site.

n

Total number of people, sum(n_per_group).

n_sites

Sites in each group (NULL with no clustering).

n_per_site

People per site in each group (NULL with no clustering); a list of each group's site sizes if they differ within a group.

deff

Design effect of each group (1 with no clustering).

n_eff

People each group would need with no clustering, keeping the groups in the same ratio as the design; for a full design, n_per_group / deff.

power

Power of the returned design.

Details

Sample size. Write \(m_1\), \(m_2\) for the effective sizes of the two groups (below). The score test in test_difference() reaches the target power when

$$z_\alpha \sqrt{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})\,(1/m_1 + 1/m_2)} + z_\beta \sqrt{p_{1,app}(1-p_{1,app})/m_1 + p_{2,app}(1-p_{2,app})/m_2} = |p_{1,app} - p_{2,app}|$$

where \(p_{g,app} = p_g \cdot Se + (1-p_g)(1-Sp)\) is the prevalence the test would measure in group \(g\), \(\bar{p} = (p_{1,app} m_1 + p_{2,app} m_2)/(m_1 + m_2)\) is the pooled prevalence the test uses, \(z_\beta\) = qnorm(power) (0.84 for 80 percent power), and \(z_\alpha\) = qnorm(1 - alpha/2) for a two-sided test (1.96 at 95 percent) or qnorm(1 - alpha) for a one-sided test (1.64 at 95 percent), with \(\alpha = 1 -\) conf_level. With no clustering and two groups of \(n\) people this is the formula of R's power.prop.test().

Because \(p_{1,app} - p_{2,app} = (p_1 - p_2)(Se + Sp - 1)\), an imperfect test shrinks the difference the test can see and increases the sample size.

Effective size. For group \(g\) with \(n_g\) people in sites of \(s_g\) people, \(m_g = n_g / D_g\) with design effect \(D_g = 1 + (s_g - 1)\,ICC_g\). For sites of different sizes, \(s_g\) is the size-weighted mean site size \(\sum s^2 / \sum s\), as in test_difference(). With one unknown \(x\), each design gives \(m_g\) directly:

No clustering

\(m_g = x\), people per group.

Fixed n_per_site1, n_per_site2

\(m_g = x \, s_g / D_g\), with \(x\) sites per group.

Fixed n_sites1, n_sites2

\(m_g = k_g x / (1 + (x - 1) ICC_g)\), with \(k_g\) sites and \(x\) people per site.

Each \(m_g\) grows with \(x\), so the left side of the equation above falls as \(x\) grows, and the function finds the smallest \(x\) that meets it with a single root search (uniroot()), then rounds up to a whole number.

Power. For a full design, or the rounded design that was solved for, the power is the equation above solved for \(z_\beta\): \(\Phi((|p_{1,app} - p_{2,app}| - z_\alpha \sqrt{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p}) (1/m_1 + 1/m_2)}) / \sqrt{p_{1,app}(1-p_{1,app})/m_1 + p_{2,app}(1-p_{2,app})/m_2})\).

Highest power. With n_sites fixed, adding people to each site cannot raise the power past a limit: each site is worth at most \(1/ICC\) independent people, so group \(g\) never counts as more than \(k_g / ICC_g\) independent people. For example, with ICC 0.05 each site is worth at most 20 independent people, so 8 sites per group give at most 160 independent people; for 10 versus 20 percent that gives 70.9 percent power, so 80 percent can never be reached. When the target is out of reach, the function stops and reports the power at that limit.

Rounding. The number of sites, or people per site, is rounded up to a whole number, the same in both groups. With n_sites fixed, every site is used, with at least 1 person each, even if fewer people would do (as in the other design functions); with n_per_site larger than needed, 1 site per group is used. The people in each group are n_sites * n_per_site, and the design effects are those of the rounded design.

References

MMS-SD Study Design Workshop. https://mrc-ide.github.io/MMS-SD_workshop/

Fleiss, J. L., Levin, B. & Paik, M. C. (2003) Statistical Methods for Rates and Proportions, 3rd ed. Wiley. (Two-group sample size.)

Kish, L. (1965) Survey Sampling. Wiley. (Design effect.)

Rogan, W. J. & Gladen, B. (1978) Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test. American Journal of Epidemiology 107(1), 71-76. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510

See also

test_difference

Examples

# Detect 10 versus 20 percent prevalence with 80 percent power
design_difference(prevalence1 = 0.10, prevalence2 = 0.20)
#> $n_per_group
#> [1] 199 199
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 398
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 199 199
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.8000726
#> 

# Higher power needs more people
design_difference(0.10, 0.20, power = 0.90)
#> $n_per_group
#> [1] 266 266
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 532
#> 
#> $n_sites

#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 266 266
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.9001549
#>
